title: Short Stuff: Madam C.J. Walker
summary: Short Stuff episode on Madam C. J. Walker (born Sarah Breedlove), a daughter of sharecroppers who became a self-made millionaire through her hair care business. The hosts cover her childhood in Louisiana and Mississippi, early marriages and widowhood, laundry work in St. Louis, the hair loss that led her to create her own formula, the Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower and related products, door-to-door sales of agents, her Harlem salon and beauty culturist network, her empowerment-focused speeches, her move to Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, and her charitable bequests to historically Black colleges and the NAACP.
topics: Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower

entities.name: Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower

segments.title: Opening and introduction to Madam C. J. Walker
segments.summary: Josh introduces the story of Madam C. J. Walker, claimed by Guinness as the first self-made female millionaire in America, and mentions the Netflix miniseries Self Made.

segments.title: Early life, marriages, and St. Louis laundry work
segments.summary: Born Sarah Breedlove on a Louisiana cotton plantation in 1867, she was orphaned young, lived with her sister in Vicksburg, Mississippi, married Moses McWilliams at fourteen, was widowed, and moved to St. Louis to do laundry. The hosts question how much her earnings were worth in today's money.

segments.title: Hair loss and the search for a product
segments.summary: In the 1890s Walker began losing her hair and found few products designed for Black women's hair. She used Poro Hair, made by Annie Turnbo Malone, and sold it briefly, then decided to develop her own formula.

segments.title: Founding the hair care company and door-to-door sales
segments.summary: Walker married Charles Joseph Walker, adopted the name Madam C. J. Walker, and launched Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower in 1906. Agents sold door to door and at churches across the South, using before-and-after photos. The reported ingredients included coconut oil, beeswax, petroleum jelly, copper sulfate, and precipitated sulfur, with sulfur as the likely active ingredient. The line expanded to a vegetable shampoo and Glossine.
topics: Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower

segments.title: Legacy debates, Harlem, and beauty culturist network
segments.summary: The hosts discuss criticism that her products emulated white beauty standards, later reassessment of her as a feminist and civil rights activist, and her divorce in 1912. She moved to Indianapolis, then Harlem, where her daughter opened a salon. She had tens of thousands of beauty culturists, held a convention in Philadelphia, and gave speeches urging Black women to demand better treatment.

segments.title: Villa Lewaro and philanthropy
segments.summary: In 1918 Walker moved to Villa Lewaro, a mansion in Irvington, New York, designed by Vertner Woodson Tandy. She died the following year. She left two-thirds of her estate to historically Black universities and to the NAACP.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh wraps the episode and gives the show credits.
